newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jordan slams Israeli settlement expansion.
newsitem.headline: Jordan slams Israeli settlement expansion.

text.p: Jordan's Crown Prince Hassan said in remarks broadcast on Saturday that Israel's expansion of Jewish settlements on occupied Arab land was unacceptable.
The prince said his country's 1994 peace treaty with Israel had suffered due to the violence that has dogged Arab-Israeli peace efforts.

"Today when you hear (of) settlements and fattening of settlements...clearly this is something that has not been accepted even in the peace treaty," the prince told Israel's Channel Two Television in an interview taped in Jordan earlier in the week.
"We do not accept any action that changes the status quo in the occupied territory," he said.
Asked if his expectations of the treaty, Israel's second with an Arab state after that with Egypt in 1979, had been met, the prince expressed reservations.

"I would be more satisfied if we were conducting this interview in Tel Aviv or Jerusalem but clearly there have been acts of violence," he said, citing violence against both Israelis and Arabs in the last year.

Prince Hassan said the opening of a second entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem in September that sparked days of clashes in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed had not helped the situation.

"It is this atmosphere, effectively, I think that has taken a lot out of the peace treaty, out of the spirit to move forward. But on the other hand I'm a realist and I think that there are so many possibilities."
The prince cited Israeli President Ezer Weizman's recent visit to Jordan, and said: "We went down to the Dead Sea Works, we saw good things being done in bad times."
Prince Hassan in September postponed a visit to Israel because he had "overburdened schedules".

Netanyahu shortly after taking office lifted a settlement building freeze the previous government had imposed on the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip where some 130,000 Jews live amidst more than two million Palestinians.
His government has approved construction of more than 3,000 new homes for Jews in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.

On Friday, Israeli officials said they had taken the first step toward building 900 more homes on the Golan Heights Israel captured from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war. They said the Israel Lands Authority was checking sites for the building.
Syria's official newspapers accused Israel on Saturday of pushing the region to war by the move.

Tensions have grown between Israel and the Palestinians and Arab states since Netanyahu took office in June. He opposes trading occupied Arab land for peace, the principle key to five years of peace talks.
